title: The harp at midnight (Berakhot 3b)
hookLine: a harp hung over David's bed; at midnight the north wind played it and he rose to study
tomorrow: is every pain sent to teach you something?

lines: HOW DO YOU KNOW IT'S MIDNIGHT?
cards: No phone, no clock, no alarm. How would you know it was exactly midnight? Roughly, maybe, by how quiet the street gets.
Exactly is harder. Berakhot asks this about King David, who says in a psalm that he rises at midnight. The Talmud's answer is a harp.

teach.b: The psalm says, in the Jewish Publication Society's old translation: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto Thee." So how did David know when midnight came? A harp hung above his bed, the Talmud says.

teach.h: THE NORTH WIND PLAYS THE HARP.
teach.b: At midnight a north wind blew through its strings and played it by itself, and David got up and studied Torah until dawn. One question for today: what is the middle of the night for?
This page answers: not only for worry, and not only for sleep. It's a time to rise toward God. The night that held grief yesterday holds music now.
Here's the unity thread. Christian scripture has a midnight of its own, in the book of Acts.

teach.h: PAUL AND SILAS SING AT MIDNIGHT.
teach.b: Paul and Silas have been beaten and locked in a prison, their feet in the stocks, and the King James Bible says: "And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them."
Two traditions, the same hour, and the same instinct: when the night is deepest, turn it toward God. The honest difference: David rises alone, woken by the wind, to study Torah.
Paul and Silas pray and sing together, in chains, and in Acts an earthquake follows.
One is a habit of learning; the other is praise under pressure. Neither story is the other's. And one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, King David's alarm clock was the wind.

how: Some Jews keep a custom of rising around midnight for prayer and study, called Tikkun Chatzot, and some Christian monastic communities keep a night office of prayer; both draw on the psalm's 'at midnight I will rise'.

games.q: what does “the harp at midnight” mean?
o: David's harp, played by the wind, waking him to study
a small harp hung over a baby's cradle as a lullaby
a harp played in the Temple for the midnight offering

p: rises and studies Torah until dawn
pray and sing in prison at midnight
at midnight I will rise to give thanks

s: the harp played by the wind is a story from the book of Psalms
the psalm says David rises at midnight; the harp and the north wind come from the Talmud, Berakhot 3b.
in Acts, Paul and Silas pray and sing at midnight in prison
and the prisoners heard them, the King James Bible says.
the Talmud and Acts tell the same story in two versions
same hour, different scenes: David studies alone; Paul and Silas sing together in chains.

games.q: a friend says the middle of the night is good for two things only: sleep or worry. what does today's page answer?
o: it can be a time to rise toward God: David's harp, Paul and Silas's songs.
only sleep; David rose because he was a king with duties to do.
only worry; yesterday's page showed even God grieving in the night.
games.why: yesterday the night held grief; today it holds music. Berakhot's David rises to study, and Acts' Paul and Silas sing: the deep night turned toward God.

practice: Sit up a little taller, the way someone does who has just decided to get out of bed. Breathe in as if wind were moving through strings, and out slowly, and let each breath be one string sounding for the whole sit.
If you'd like to try David's habit, set tomorrow's alarm a few minutes early and give those minutes to something you want to learn.

wordCard.voice: The harp at midnight. David's harp, played by the north wind, waking him to study until dawn.

orig.note: Hebrew: a harp or lyre, David's instrument, played at midnight by the north wind.

carryVoice: Here's the line: the harp at midnight, a wind that wakes you for something good. Berakhot, day three.
